paper_title: Challenges and interventions in water resource management for horticultural crop production in rural and tribal communities in India

paper_identity.paper_title: Challenges and interventions in water resource management for horticultural crop production in rural and tribal communities in India

paper_summary: This mixed-methods case study in Ransai village (Raigad, Maharashtra) combines FGDs, transect walks, participant observation, March 2024 soil testing, and CropWat 8.0 analysis of bitter gourd and other horticultural crops. It documents dry-season water scarcity despite high annual rainfall, dominance of flood/furrow irrigation with low system efficiency, limited rainwater harvesting, structural barriers to micro-irrigation adoption, and a yield gap versus potential under better water management.
study_region: Ransai village, Uran taluka, Raigad district, Maharashtra, India (Konkan; panchayat area 1631.64 ha)
study_period: Field work February 2024; irrigation observations 2022–2023 seasons; long-term climate for CropWat; soil tests March 2024
methodology: Qualitative participatory methods (FGDs n=6, transect walks, participant observation, resource mapping) plus CropWat 8.0 crop water assessment and laboratory soil analysis (0–30 cm).
paper_type_rationale: Single tribal village deep dive with triangulated qualitative evidence and site-specific CropWat/soil data rather than broad statistical causal identification.

key_relationships: Maharashtra monsoon supplies ~80% of annual precipitation; non-monsoon horticulture relies on irrigation (cited state context).
Raigad district rainfall cited 2000–3000 mm/year mainly monsoon yet summer water scarcity due to storage/runoff dynamics.
Farmers apply 252 m³/season vs CropWat gross 213.46 m³ for bitter gourd on 0.16 ha (over-application linked to low WUE and leaching).
Government micro-irrigation subsidies cited 55–75% in discussion (policy lever, not village-specific outcome).

limitations: Qualitative causal claims are triangulated but not econometrically identified; CropWat results are for representative crop schedules; some policy examples are from other states cited for intervention design.

important_variables.significance: CropWat quantifies large gap between effective rainfall and irrigation requirement for the vegetable season, anchoring dry-season scarcity for horticulture.
Furrow efficiency 70% and measured over-irrigation versus model gross requirement explain water waste and nutrient leaching narrative.
~90% rainfall loss from lack of harvesting/storage is central to why high annual rainfall does not buffer dry-season irrigation stress.
Non-adoption of drip/sprinkler is the key behavioral/technology node linking cultural, credit, land, and extension barriers to inefficient irrigation.
Reported bitter gourd yield gap motivates the water-management intervention framing.

important_variables_narrative: The study’s quantitative spine is CropWat-based irrigation demand versus effective rainfall for horticultural crops, combined with measured over-application under furrow irrigation and low system efficiency. Qualitative evidence stresses missing rainwater storage, fragmented holdings, credit exclusion, and weak extension as barriers to micro-irrigation. Together these explain persistent dry-season scarcity and groundwater/storage stress despite a humid annual rainfall regime, and the observed yield gap for bitter gourd.
